claims.text: Applying a nanoscale 2D transition-metal-dichalcogenide high-entropy lubricant coating to an HEA will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide service-temperature range.
The proposed substrate is an untreated bulk CoCrFeMnNi-type HEA with its standard microstructure and no engineered surface-lubrication features.
(MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 is an example of the proposed 2D high-entropy lubricant.
Air-spray or a similar deposition process can produce a thin, uniform coating with good adhesion on the HEA surface.
The coating is expected to remain tribologically effective from room temperature to approximately 800 °C.
The coating is expected to remain effective under normal loads of approximately 1–9 N.
Sliding forms an in situ tribocatalytically active, shearable nanocomposite surface layer.
Within the surface layer, the 2D nanolubricant becomes aligned and intimately bonded to the substrate.
The 2D coating physically separates the contacting surfaces and provides a stable, low-shear interface.
The coating's tribochemical activity generates a lubricious tribofilm during sliding.
Physical separation and tribofilm formation reduce interfacial shear stress.
Reduced interfacial shear suppresses adhesive and abrasive wear.
Relative to an untreated HEA tested under identical conditions, the coated HEA will have lower average friction and lower wear.
The coating may reduce wear rate by one to two orders of magnitude.
The intervention remains effective only while the coating adheres robustly and survives mechanical loading and thermal cycling.
Delamination or severe coating deformation will degrade tribological performance.
Coated and untreated samples will be compared by identical ball-on-disk tests at room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C and at loads from 1 to 9 N.
Friction coefficient, wear-track depth or volume, and coating integrity are measurable experimental outcomes.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both friction and wear across the tested temperature range, using an order-of-magnitude improvement as an example threshold, will falsify the hypothesis.
The numerical improvement and durability under prolonged cyclic loading remain uncertain and may depend on coating uniformity and adhesion.
